claims.text: Yield strength in the quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy becomes insensitive to strain rate between 300 and 500 K.
The proposed strain-rate-insensitive regime is caused by thermally activated dislocation glide over short-range solute obstacles.
Below 150 K or above a strain rate of 10^3 s^-1, deformation shifts to athermic dislocation nucleation.
Below 150 K or above a strain rate of 10^3 s^-1, stress-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation may become active.
The low-temperature or high-rate mechanism shift causes a sharp increase in yield strength.
The low-temperature or high-rate mechanism shift causes increased strain-rate sensitivity.
The initial alloy is a single-phase FCC random solid solution without pre-existing precipitates or coherent interfaces.
Plastic deformation involves evolution of dislocation density.
Partial-dislocation nucleation can produce stacking-fault networks and HCP transformation nuclei.
At intermediate temperatures, dislocation glide is thermally activated and rate-sensitive.
In CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, constituent lattice-parameter differences create friction that hinders partial-dislocation motion.
At low temperature or high strain rate, lattice-friction stress or the phase-transformation barrier dominates and decouples yield strength from thermal activation.
Yield-strength-versus-strain-rate curves exhibit a plateau between 300 and 500 K.
Yield strength rises steeply at 77 K or at high strain rates.
HCP signatures should appear in TEM or XRD when the phase-transformation mechanism operates.
Standard FCC alloys generally follow a power-law dependence of yield strength on strain rate across all temperatures without phase transformation.
Secondary phases or coherent interfaces can alter the deformation mechanisms relative to a single-phase FCC alloy.
The hierarchically patterned FCC/B2 Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy activates dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and deformation twins.
CoNiCrFeMn nanowires undergo FCC-to-HCP transformation during simulated tensile deformation at 77 K.
Cr or Mo additions may induce Laves phases or carbides in the target alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome attribute a strain-rate-insensitive plateau to thermally activated glide, while the mechanism field explicitly characterizes that same intermediate-temperature glide as rate-sensitive.

The hypothesis predicts increased strain-rate sensitivity after the low-temperature/high-rate transition, whereas the mechanism describes the resulting strength as decoupled from thermal activation; the relationship between these assertions is not resolved.
